standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: Content negotiation is the HTTP handshake where the client says what format it wants and the server decides if it can deliver.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: Content negotiation is the process where a client and server agree on the data format. The client sends an Accept header saying what format it wants in the response. Spring looks through its registered HttpMessageConverters to find one that can produce that format.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: There are two directions to this. The Accept header controls what format comes back in the response — the server selects a converter to serialize the output. The Content-Type header describes what format the client is sending in the request body — the server selects a converter to deserialize the input.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: Accept: application/json: client wants JSON back — Spring uses Jackson.
Accept: application/xml: client wants XML — Spring needs jackson-dataformat-xml.
Content-Type: application/json: client is sending JSON — Jackson deserializes it.
406 Not Acceptable: no registered converter can produce the requested format.
415 Unsupported Media Type: no registered converter can read the incoming Content-Type.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: If the client doesn't send an Accept header, Spring defaults to JSON when Jackson is configured. Many developers don't know content negotiation is even happening because JSON just works by default. The mechanism only becomes visible when clients request a different format or send an unsupported Content-Type.

cap: Use the produces attribute on your mapping annotations to explicitly declare what formats an endpoint supports, rather than relying on global negotiation silently.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: produces and consumes are how you declare your endpoint's content type contract explicitly — instead of leaving it to Spring's defaults.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: produces restricts what response formats this endpoint can output. Spring checks it against the client's Accept header. If they don't match, the request is rejected with 406 before your method is even called.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: consumes restricts what request body formats this endpoint will accept. Spring checks it against the client's Content-Type header. If they don't match, the request is rejected with 415 before your method is called.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: Use MediaType constants instead of raw strings — MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE instead of the string 'application/json'. Constants avoid typos and give IDE autocomplete. Multiple formats are supported: an array of values in produces means the endpoint can serve both JSON and XML.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: non-obvious: produces and consumes can be set at the class level on @RequestMapping to apply to all methods in a controller. You'd typically do this if your entire controller is JSON-only, rather than repeating it on every method.

cap: Without specifying produces, Spring uses global content negotiation with all registered converters. Specifying produces makes the contract explicit and the API self-documenting.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: spring-boot-starter-web already includes Jackson — Spring Boot wires it up without a single line of configuration from you.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: When spring-boot-starter-web is on the classpath, Spring Boot's JacksonAutoConfiguration activates. It creates a default ObjectMapper bean, registers MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, and makes JSON the default response format for all @RestController methods.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: You can customize the ObjectMapper through application.properties without writing any code. Setting spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false makes dates serialize as ISO strings. Setting spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=NON_NULL skips null fields in every response.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: application.properties: configure global ObjectMapper behavior — indent output, date format, null handling.
@Bean ObjectMapper: define your own bean for full control — Spring Boot backs off and uses yours.
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer: add to the auto-configured settings without replacing them entirely.
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown=true): on a DTO class — silently ignore unknown fields during deserialization.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: sharp edge: Defining an @Bean ObjectMapper replaces the entire auto-configured one. You lose any customizations Boot applied. For most cases, Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer is the safer choice — it applies on top of the auto-configuration rather than replacing it.

cap: JavaTimeModule handles Java 8 LocalDate and LocalDateTime serialization. Spring Boot usually auto-registers it — verify by testing a date field in your response.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: MediaType constants are the type-safe way to reference MIME types — no more typos in 'application/json'.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: MediaType is a Spring class that provides constants for MIME type strings. Instead of hardcoding the string 'application/json' in your annotations — which can be misspelled — you use MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE.

beats.label: parts_or_states
beats.content: There are two forms to know. The VALUE variant — like APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE — is a plain String constant. Use it in annotation attributes like produces and consumes. The non-VALUE variant — like APPLICATION_JSON — is a MediaType object. Use it when calling methods that take a MediaType parameter, like HttpHeaders.setContentType.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE: for REST API responses — the most common.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: non-obvious: A common mistake is using APPLICATION_JSON where APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE is needed and vice versa. If you see a compile error that a String was expected but a MediaType was provided, you need the _VALUE variant. If you see that a MediaType was expected but a String was provided, drop the _VALUE suffix.

cap: Using constants over string literals is a small thing that prevents bugs and makes code searchable — refactoring tools can find all usages of APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, but not all hardcoded strings.
followup_handoff: What is the difference between MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON and MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE?

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: Content-Type and Accept are both HTTP headers about data format — but they point in opposite directions.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: Content-Type describes the format of the data being sent right now. The client sets it on a POST or PUT request body to say 'this is JSON I'm sending you'. The server sets it on the response to say 'this is JSON I'm sending back'.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: Accept is a preference declaration. The client sets it to say 'this is the format I want in your response'. The server uses it to pick the right serializer.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: In a typical POST: Content-Type: application/json tells Spring to deserialize the request body with Jackson. Accept: application/json tells Spring to serialize the response with Jackson. They often match, but they don't have to — a client could send XML and want JSON back.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: gotcha: If a client sends a POST with a JSON body but forgets to set Content-Type: application/json, Spring can't determine the format and may return 415 Unsupported Media Type. This is one of the most common mistakes when testing APIs with curl or Postman for the first time.

cap: In Spring: consumes checks the incoming Content-Type. produces checks the incoming Accept header. The directions mirror the headers.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: Adding XML support to a Spring Boot REST API is literally one dependency — no controller changes required.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: Add the jackson-dataformat-xml dependency to your pom.xml. Spring Boot auto-detects it and registers an XML message converter. Your existing @RestController methods now serve both JSON and XML — the client's Accept header chooses the format.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Jackson's XML module reuses the same annotations you already have. @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, and @JsonInclude all work for XML output too. You don't need to add separate JAXB annotations or @XmlRootElement on every class.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: Accept: application/json: existing behavior, JSON response.
Accept: application/xml: new behavior after adding the dependency, XML response.
@JacksonXmlRootElement(localName='user'): customize the XML root element name.
@JacksonXmlProperty: rename an XML element, similar to @JsonProperty.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: non-obvious: Before adding the XML dependency, a client sending Accept: application/xml gets 406 Not Acceptable. After adding it, they get XML. This is transparent — existing JSON clients are unaffected because their Accept: application/json still routes to the Jackson JSON converter as before.

cap: XML support is rarely needed in modern REST APIs — most clients speak JSON. But knowing how to add it shows you understand content negotiation at a deeper level.
